title: The Hare in the Moon
bigQuestion: What does the hare's gift teach about giving what you can?

story.title: Four Friends and a Gift
story.kicker: The hare comes back with nothing but an idea.
paragraphs: Buddhists tell this Jataka tale. Four friends lived by a forest. They were a hare, a monkey, a jackal and an otter. They wanted to give a gift to anyone in need.
One day a hungry traveler came by. The otter found fish. The jackal found some food. The monkey picked mangoes. Each friend had something to give.
The hare only ate grass. People cannot eat grass. The hare thought and thought. Then he had an idea. "I will give myself," he said.
The traveler made a fire. The hare jumped in. But the fire felt cool as snow! The traveler was really Sakka, a king of the gods in the story. He was testing the friends.
story.think: Why was the hare's gift so surprising?

lessons.title: Hare, Monkey, Jackal, Otter
lessons.mainIdea: Four animal friends in the Hare Jataka each wanted to give a gift.
reading: This tale is called the Hare Jataka. It is Jataka number 316. Buddhists tell that the wise hare was the Buddha in an earlier life.
The hare had three friends. They were a monkey, a jackal and an otter. The hare taught them to be kind and to share.

words.d: an animal like a big rabbit with long ears
a furry animal that swims and catches fish

look.title: What Each Friend Found
rows: friends who found food for a person
look.cite: Jataka no. 316, Sasa Jataka, in The Jataka, ed. E.B. Cowell, vol. 3 (1897)
look.prompt: How many friends found food a person could eat?

check.why: The Hare Jataka tells of a hare, a monkey, a jackal and an otter.

check.q: Who was the Buddha-to-be in this tale?
check.why: Buddhists tell that the wise hare was the Buddha in an earlier life.
An otter is a furry animal that swims and catches fish.

lessons.title: Finding Gifts
lessons.mainIdea: Each friend found food to share, except the hare.
reading: The otter found fish in the river. The jackal found some food. The monkey picked sweet mangoes from a tree.
The hare looked around. He only had grass. He knew a person could not eat grass. What could he give?

words.d: to give some of what you have to others

look.title: Only Grass
look.text: Look at the hare in the field. His friends run past carrying fish and fruit. He sits in the green grass. His ears go up. He is thinking hard.
look.prompt: What do you think the hare feels?

check.why: In the tale, the monkey picked mangoes.
The hare ate grass, which a person could not eat.

choices: give some of what you have
check.why: To share means to give some of what you have to others.

lessons.title: Giving Himself
lessons.mainIdea: In the tale, the hare offered himself because he had nothing else.
reading: The hare wanted to give something. He had only himself. So he offered himself as food for the traveler.
The traveler lit a fire. The hare jumped in. But the tale says the fire did not burn him at all. It felt as cool as snow.

words.d: to hold something out for someone to take

look.title: The Fire Was Cool
look.text: The hare leaped into the fire, glad to give. But the flames did not even warm a single hair. It felt like jumping into snow.
look.cite: Jataka no. 316, Sasa Jataka, retold from The Jataka, ed. E.B. Cowell, vol. 3 (1897)
look.prompt: What surprising thing happened in the fire?

check.why: With no food to give, the hare offered himself.
The tale says the fire did not burn him and felt cool.

choices: hold out for someone to take
check.why: To offer is to hold something out for someone to take.

lessons.title: Sakka's Test
lessons.mainIdea: The traveler was Sakka, who was testing the hare's kindness.
reading: The traveler was not really a traveler. The tale says he was Sakka, a king of the gods. He came to test the four friends.
Sakka saw that the hare's kindness was real. He did not let the hare be hurt. He praised the hare's big heart.

words.d: a king of the gods in Buddhist stories

look.title: A Hidden Visitor
look.text: Many stories have a visitor in disguise. The visitor looks plain. At the end, we learn who they really are. Then we see why they came.
look.prompt: Why do you think Sakka came in disguise?

check.why: The tale says the traveler was Sakka in disguise.
Sakka came to test their kindness.
In the tale, Sakka kept the hare safe.

lessons.title: A Picture on the Moon
lessons.mainIdea: The tale says Sakka painted the hare on the moon so all would remember.
reading: Sakka wanted everyone to remember the hare's gift. The tale says he drew the shape of a hare on the moon.
Look at the full moon. Some dark spots look like a rabbit. Buddhists tell this tale to explain the picture.

words.d: the round light we see in the night sky

look.title: The Full Moon
look.text: Look at the full moon on a clear night. It is round and bright. There are gray shapes on it. Some people see a face. Some see a rabbit with long ears.
look.prompt: What shape do you see when you look at the moon?

check.q: What did Sakka draw on the moon?
check.why: The tale says Sakka drew the hare on the moon.

choices: so all would remember the gift
check.why: He wanted everyone to remember the hare's kindness.

check.q: When can you best see the rabbit shape?
check.why: The shape shows best on the bright full moon.

lessons.title: Moon Rabbits Around the World
lessons.mainIdea: People in Japan, China and other places also tell of a rabbit in the moon.
reading: In Japan and China, people also tell about a rabbit in the moon. In some stories the rabbit makes rice cakes or medicine.
Many families look at the moon at the fall moon festival. They share treats. They think about giving what you can.

words.d: a special day when people gather to celebrate

look.title: A Moon Festival
look.text: Look at a family on a porch in the fall. The moon is big and round. A grandma points up and tells about the rabbit in the moon. Everyone shares round cakes.
look.prompt: What might the family be thinking about as they look at the moon?

check.q: Where else do people tell of a moon rabbit?
check.why: Moon rabbit stories are told in Japan, China and other places.

check.q: What does the rabbit make in some stories?
check.why: In some Japanese and Chinese stories the rabbit makes rice cakes or medicine.
A festival is a special day when people gather to celebrate.

review.why: This tale is the Sasa Jataka, the Hare Jataka, no. 316.

review.q: Why did the hare offer himself?
choices: he had nothing else to give
review.why: He had only grass, so he gave the only thing he had.
The tale says Sakka came in disguise to test them.
The tale says the fire did not burn the hare.

review.q: Where did Sakka draw the hare?
review.why: The tale says Sakka drew the hare on the moon.
Buddhists tell the Hare Jataka to teach giving.
